body_text: Dyson wants to replicate the success of its vacuums and hair products but in your mouth. So far it is not going so well. The company’s $500 Camerajet toothbrush (powered by AI, of course) sprayed water across the bathroom and then stopped working, according to one Bloomberg reporter who tested the product . It was also incredibly hard to find stocked in any major retailer, they reported. Stocks ended a rocky week down on Friday. Elon Musk has found another way for his two companies to collaborate, leaving some wondering whether a more formal union could be next. On Thursday, CEO Elon Musk unveiled the long-awaited second-generation Tesla Roadster, a sports car developed with the help of his rocket company SpaceX . During a demonstration in Texas, the vehicle drove upside down, flipped through the air, and jumped over a row of other Teslas using rocket-style thrusters powered by compressed air. The company says the Roadster can accelerate from zero to 60 mph in less than a second, reach speeds exceeding 230 mph, and travel more than 300 miles on a single charge. “You’re going to see some crazy stuff tonight,” said Musk, who is CEO of both companies. “You’re going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company.” Deliveries for the long-delayed vehicle aren't expected until 2028. (The second gen Roadster was first announced by Musk in 2017 with delivery slated for 2020. Tesla's reservation agreement explicitly says the company cannot guarantee when the Roadster will be delivered or whether it will be delivered at all.) Musk also said he was "not sure it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions." It will almost certainly spark some sort of regulatory review from the Federal Aviation Administration, Wired points out . But the Roadster's biggest significance may have less to do with its ability to fly than with the company helping it get off the ground. The unveiling has added fuel to speculation that Musk could eventually combine Tesla and SpaceX, bringing his electric-car business and rocket company under one roof. Prediction market traders increased the odds of a merger being announced by early next year. One Barclays analyst predicted that such a merger could happen before the end of this year. The Roadster is unlikely to do much for Tesla's bottom line. Musk has previously described the Roadster as a "small potato situation" that would not "move the needle in a major way financially." Tesla reports earnings this week, with analysts penciling in $19.6 billion in quarterly automotive sales, a 7.5% decline from the same period last year. As Tesla's traditional car business faces pressure, Musk is increasingly pitching investors on a future built around AI and robotics — areas where his companies' ambitions overlap. Veteran tech analyst Gene Munster put it best in an X post : “Two takeaways from tonight’s Roadster event. It was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers. Elon can’t wait to bring $TSLA and $SPCX together.” The cumulative market capitalization for quantum computing companies IonQ , D-Wave , and Rigetti is virtually unchanged from where it was in early September 2025, right before those companies ramped in part on speculation over US government support. The fundamentals of the industry at large really haven’t meaningfully improved over the past year, nor have they deteriorated. And quantum computing is not a space where most traders were looking for hockey-stick growth now, it’s more about the prospect for technological breakthroughs that have the potential to spur parabolic operational improvements further down the road. The key underlying factor may be that the speculative energy just is not there anymore for this part of the market. Major pure-play quantum computing companies that have been around for a few years (like IonQ, D-Wave, and Rigetti) have seen call volumes drop precipitously from their 2025 peaks. While there are some nascent signs of potential risk-defined falling-knife-catching in some of these names via options lately, it’s nothing to write home about yet. — Luke Kawa, read the rest in EntryPoint Go deeper with EntryPoint . body_text: It’s a boom time for Advent calendars, with wholesale sales of the countdown-to-Christmas products up 63% year over year. The holiday tradition, where kids can get perhaps a chocolate or a small toy each day in the season of Advent ahead of the big day, has wound up at the confluence of a couple of major toy-industry trends . What is an Advent calendar if not 24 blind boxes you get to crack open? Is the thrill not the same as that of opening up a trading card pack or a video game lootbox? And with adults now buying most of the toys for themselves, anyway, what could play better to a “kidult” audience than an ostensibly religious way to give yourself toys for a whole month? Coreweave had a wild week, with anxieties about its debt spurred by a rather candid comment by one of its founders — and stoked by Elon Musk — spiraling into a broader moment of anxiety around just how much money the AI revolution is requiring investors to put up. A full-court press from CoreWeave’s boosters appeared to reset expectations , but where does this all leave us as we assess the state of the AI trade? CoreWeave shares sold off as much as 15% on Wednesday after a remark from a cofounder about the company’s attempts to get an investment-grade rating that would allow it to borrow from insurers rattled markets, with the executive describing the capital as “unlimited, like, that’s all the money in the world that sits in the insurance tranche.” That put a bit of a spotlight on the company’s debt situation, as the 2031 CoreWeave bonds yield 15%, which is very very high for a company in its position. Well, amid the renewed scrutiny the cost of protecting that debt against default for five years rose to 1,194 basis points , 74.5 basis points in a day, swaps pricing in a 60% chance of default within five years. Wow , one might think, even Elon Musk is worried about the AI bubble? No. No he is not. Don’t be ridiculous. Elon Musk simply owns a competitor: SpaceX is rapidly attempting to build out large AI data centers that can both reduce its reliance on — and ultimately compete with — neoclouds like CoreWeave. In fact, as Grok and the other products of SpaceX’s AI lab continue to lag rival products out of Anthropic, OpenAI, Alphabet , Meta and so on, the core shareholder value of SpaceX’s AI business will be the neocloud element that can eventually sell compute to those winning teams. Remember, SpaceX cut a $1 billion a month deal to sell compute in September, which of course leads to the question of “why does SpaceX have excess compute?” Elon’s “yikes” is, if anything, more kicking a rival when they’re down rather than any concession that the technology he has tied his fortune to has issues. So, where does that leave us? Well, CoreWeave stock finished up 5% Thursday, still down 17% over the five-day, with its CEO waving the week away saying “there will be periods of time when the market misunderstands and acts irrationally.” The unique cultures of Silicon Valley and Wall Street have been in general alignment that the AI boom is going to make a lot of people a lot of money. But before we get cocky, it’s worth remembering two axioms held as truth in either camp that apply very well : From the West coast: the future is already here — it's just not very evenly distributed. From the East coast: markets can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent. The AI boom’s benefits to shareholders will not necessarily be evenly distributed. If, for instance, there are one or two models that get a lot of pickup or achieve milestones faster than rivals can achieve, even companies that get lots of money in investment will not be worth a whole lot. If the world runs all its AI out of data centers, the neoclouds win; if, on the other hand, we don’t need all these buildings and you can eventually run a solid model on a phone, then the neoclouds will bite it. Heck, maybe free Chinese open source models can do 97% of the work of AI, and the American labs become boutique R&D firms arguing with academics over whether they actually solved theoretical math problems. In short: There are lots of worlds in which both LLMs are popular, useful technologies integrated into the American economy, and also some of the companies getting high valuations don’t exist anymore. Sure, which companies win and which companies lose that future could be decided by breakthroughs in AI model development or a phalanx of Nvidia chips powered by fusion power or a data center deployed to space, or any of these big and exciting reasons that a company might win that investors like to imagine. But for lots of them, their victory or their death will be decided by the rather boring parts of the balance sheet describing how much money they owe creditors in 2032. Whether this week was actually the axis upon which the AI trade turns is a bit premature. But it is the shape of things to come, a taste of what the future will at some point bring, at least when everyone flips their cards on the table and the winnings get divided. Just because your business model was the beating heart of the AI industry in 2026 doesn’t prevent you from being the bloated, doomed appendix of the AI industry in 2032. Not every buzzy well-funded company’s gonna make it. Just ask Character.ai . body_text: Google dropped its annual Halloween “ Frightgeist ” data earlier today, revealing the costumes, candy, decor, and more that have spiked in popularity this year. Unsurprisingly, this year’s movies are playing a big part in the trending outfits of 2026, with Agamemnon from “The Odyssey” in fourth; Nikki from “Obsession” in third; and Buddy the Unicorn, the titular character from the viral horror phenomenon “Buddy,” taking first. The highest trending kids’ costumes this year have gone in a different direction, however, with the top two spots taken by country stars: apparently you can expect to greet swarms of younger trick-or-treaters dressed as Ella Langley and the late Dolly Parton this October 31. Stocks had a particularly rough day on Wednesday, with the S&P 500 falling by a little more than a point and the Nasdaq 100 falling 1.9% Never mind that it’s basically a huge Apple Watch! Never mind that it’s yet another screen to add to your roster! Never mind that “iPad” might just have been the perfect name for an Apple home hub had it not been taken in 2010! Just be happy that you now have a new option in the crowded market of big tech smart-home products to choose from, after Apple unveiled its HomeView smart display yesterday. Dubbed a “new way to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage the home,” the 7-inch, $299 device will officially drop on Friday, November 13, per the company’s announcement . From the chaotic three-minute trailer, users will be able to play music, control smart devices, FaceTime hands-free, and access Siri AI — basically everything you can do from any number of the smaller Apple devices you already own, cementing the pithy “ It’s an iPhone for your home .” verdict from The Verge’s Jennifer Pattison Tuohy. Alongside another device to take to battle against Google and Amazon equivalents, Apple also announced new HomePod smart speakers, a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, and a suite of smart-home accessories made in collaboration with LG. Increasing its offering of devices to dot around the house makes sense when taking a look at its Apple’s Wearables, Home and Accessories segment more broadly. The division that covers AirPods, Watches, TVs, Beats, and accessories like chargers and cases has seen revenues sink a little in recent years, with sales down some $3.2 billion in the first quarter of the year compared to their 2022 peak. It’s important to note that even with the declines more broadly, Apple’s Wearables, Home and Accessories unit still hauled $7.9 billion for the company in Q3 — putting it slightly behind Macs ($10.4 billion), slightly ahead of iPads ($6.2 billion), and contributing 7.6% of the company’s overall revenues for the quarter. With reportedly soft sales for the company’s latest iPhone and the big bet it’s placed on its soon-to-be-released foldable Duo not yet a surefire success, could the company’s new range of home products rise to the challenge and potentially help CEO John Ternus keep the Apple house in order? As we all know by now, getting to the bottom of one online recipe is troubling enough — fighting through ads and meandering asides about what the dish really represents to the author. So, sheets.works has really put the work in with a new Data Drop exploring the most common recipes across 2.2 million online recipes. The chief finding from the ambitious project? We might be decidedly uninspired in the kitchen, with chicken casserole emerging as the nation’s leading dish on the internet, as cooks across the country look to the 20th century staple to fill up midweek meal slots or fill Thanksgiving tables. More broadly, around one in every 26 recipes that sheets.works assessed contained the word “casserole,” with broccoli and squash casseroles coming in as the second most written-down dishes online. The full project is heavy on data viz and contains other insights on everything from the most common individual ingredients, popular flavor combinations, and roughly how many components the average dish contains (~seven to eight, apparently)... Any sense of relief wasn’t to last however, as online audiences happily pounced on Zuck’s appearance on The Cheeky Pint podcast earlier this week. However, it wasn’t a misplaced comment or tense entanglement with the host, Stripe co-founder John Collison, that drew attention to the founder and CEO; it was his apparent struggle to stomach the customary “Cheeky Pint” (568 milliliters of the black stuff).
